summary: The bill pauses all new H-1B visas for three years and then permanently caps them at 25,000 per year while requiring a $100,000 employer fee, $200,000 minimum wage, three-year maximum stay, highest-wage priority instead of a lottery, and bans on dual intent, family accompaniment, third-party staffing, federal hiring, OPT work authorization, and adjustment to permanent residency.

scores.thoughts: The bill imposes a new $100,000 employer fee on H-1B petitions that is deposited into the Treasury, but it does not authorize, expand, or reduce any government spending programs. The fee is a revenue measure rather than a spending provision, so the bill has no meaningful bearing on government spending levels.

Section 3(c) creates a new $100,000 per-petition fee on employers filing H-1B petitions. This functions as an additional financial burden on (primarily corporate) users of the program and therefore moves slightly in the direction of higher effective taxation on employers, but it is a targeted visa fee rather than a broad tax policy change.
The bill contains no provisions related to healthcare delivery, insurance, public coverage, or market-based reforms.
The bill contains no provisions related to firearms, background checks, or gun regulations.

The bill is almost entirely devoted to immigration reform. It imposes a three-year pause on new H-1B visas, cuts the annual cap from 85,000 to 25,000, shortens visa duration, adds a $100k fee, raises the wage floor to $200k, ends dual intent, prohibits third-party and concurrent employment, eliminates OPT, and bars adjustment of status for most nonimmigrants. These are comprehensive, restrictive changes to a major temporary immigration pathway, strongly aligning with the +1 pole of restricting immigration.
The bill contains no provisions related to abortion access or restrictions.
The bill contains no provisions related to military or defense spending or policy.
The bill contains no provisions related to environmental regulations or climate policy.
The bill contains no provisions related to welfare programs, food stamps, or other safety-net benefits.

Section 6 eliminates the Optional Practical Training (OPT) program for F, M, and J visa holders, but this is an immigration-employment measure rather than an education-policy change involving school funding, curriculum, or choice programs.
The bill contains no provisions related to drug enforcement or decriminalization.
The bill contains no provisions related to sentencing, policing, or criminal-justice reform.
While H-1B visas affect the cross-border movement of skilled labor, the bill does not address tariffs, trade agreements, or globalization policy.
The new $100k fee would generate revenue that could marginally reduce deficits, but the bill does not address debt reduction targets, deficit spending, or fiscal policy.
The bill contains no provisions related to LGBTQ+ legal protections.
The bill contains no provisions related to foreign aid.
The bill contains no provisions related to voting access or election integrity.
Although H-1B visas are frequently used in the tech sector, the bill addresses only visa issuance and labor-market protections, not data privacy, platform regulation, or tech oversight.

Multiple provisions (new wage floor of $200k, attestation that U.S. workers are unavailable and will not be adversely affected, prohibition on layoffs in the prior/following 12 months, and elimination of the lottery in favor of highest-wage offers) are explicitly designed to protect U.S. workers' wages and employment conditions. This aligns modestly with the -1 direction of stronger worker protections.
The bill contains no provisions related to religious exemptions or civil-rights enforcement.
